title: Scheduling work with cron
objective: By the end of this lesson you can schedule a script to run unattended, read the schedule syntax without guessing, and diagnose the reason a scheduled job fails when the same command works by hand.

blocks.text: cron is the part of the system that runs commands on a schedule. Backups, log rotation, certificate renewal, cleanup — the unglamorous work that keeps a server healthy happens here. It is also where a script that works perfectly by hand mysteriously fails, for reasons that are entirely predictable once you know them.

rows: 01:30 on the first day of every month
Every hour from 09:00 to 17:00, Monday to Friday

blocks.caption: Managing your own schedule
lines: crontab -r      # remove ALL of your entries — careful, there is no confirmation

blocks.title: Why your job fails on schedule but works by hand
blocks.text: cron runs your command with a nearly empty environment: a minimal PATH, no variables from your shell profile, and the home directory as the working directory. Every 'it works when I run it' mystery traces back to one of those three. Use absolute paths for every command and every file, and set what you need explicitly at the top of the script.
Capture the output or you are flying blind

blocks.caption: Always log a scheduled job
lines: # Without 2>&1 the error messages are the part you lose —
# which is precisely the part you needed.

blocks.text: By default cron tries to email you its output, which on most machines goes nowhere. Redirecting to a log file makes the job's history readable with the same tools you already know: tail -f while it runs, grep to find failures afterwards.

blocks.title: Test the schedule without waiting for it
blocks.text: Run the exact command line from your crontab by hand first, with the same absolute paths. Then temporarily schedule it for two minutes from now and watch the log. Never wait until 02:00 to find out you had a typo.

Most modern distributions also ship systemd timers, which do the same job with more features: dependencies, resource limits, catching up on a run that was missed while the machine was off, and logs that go to the system journal. cron remains everywhere and stays the right tool for something simple, but if you see a .timer unit on a server, that is what it is.

blocks.caption: Reading what a system already schedules
lines: systemctl list-timers --all     # every timer and when it next fires
journalctl -u backup.service    # the logs of what one unit did

blocks.title: Scheduled jobs are a security surface
blocks.text: A scheduled task runs by itself, often as root, and nobody reads it again after the day it was created. That combination is exactly what an attacker wants: edit the script the job runs — a script that is 777 will do nicely — and their code executes with the job's privileges on the job's schedule. When you inspect a machine, reading its crontabs and timers is not optional.

blocks.title: Schedule something and watch it run
steps: Run: crontab -l                       (see what you already have — probably nothing)
Wait two minutes, then run: cat /tmp/cron-test.log
Run: crontab -e  and remove that line again
Run: systemctl list-timers --all | head        (what the system schedules for itself)
Run: ls -l /etc/cron.daily/                    (the daily maintenance jobs on this machine)
blocks.expected: An empty crontab, then a log file gaining a timestamp every two minutes, then a clean removal. Finally, the system's own scheduled work — which on most machines includes log rotation and package cleanup you never set up yourself.

cheatsheet: Five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
crontab -e edit · crontab -l list · crontab -r deletes everything with no confirmation
cron has a minimal PATH and no profile — use absolute paths everywhere
Test the exact command by hand, then schedule it two minutes out to verify
Read crontabs and timers when inspecting a machine — they run unattended, often as root

checkpoint.prompt: A script runs perfectly when you type it, but fails every night from cron. What is the first thing to check?

choices.B: Whether the script uses relative paths or relies on environment variables that cron does not provide
choices.C: Whether the machine reboots at night
choices.D: Whether the file is owned by root

checkpoint.explanation: cron gives a minimal PATH, no shell profile, and a different working directory. Absolute paths and explicitly set variables remove the whole class of failure.

checkpoint.prompt: Why append 2>&1 to a scheduled command?

choices.A: It runs the job twice for reliability
choices.B: It sends error messages to the same log as normal output, so a failure leaves a readable trace
choices.D: It gives the job higher priority

checkpoint.explanation: Without it you capture only the normal output and lose the errors — the exact part you need when diagnosing why last night's run did nothing.

checkpoint.prompt: Why are scheduled jobs worth inspecting during a security review?

choices.A: They consume most of the CPU
choices.B: They run unattended and often as root, so a modified script executes an attacker's code on a schedule with those privileges
choices.D: They always run as the user who created them and are therefore harmless

checkpoint.explanation: Unattended, privileged, and rarely re-read. A writable script referenced by a root cron entry is a complete escalation path on its own.
